Lecture 8 — The Expected Value and Variance of a Random Variable, and the Rules for E and V

The expected value of a discrete random variable is built up from flipping three coins, the variance is defined the same way, and both get rules for what happens when a variable is multiplied by a constant or shifted.

3The idealized population and μ

Another way to think of the expected value is to think of it as the mean of an idealized population in which each value occurs exactly as frequently as it should based on the probabilities.

We often denote by writing or by .

If we [are] studying a real world population and measures some value for population members, then the real world population is the idealized population for the random variable and is the mean for this population (with respect to the value measured).

✎ Explanation (added)

Why this is the same idea. The eight runs "exactly as expected" on the first boards were an idealized population for the coin : eight members with values 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3. Its mean, computed the Lecture 2 way as , is 1.5. So and the population mean are the same number, which is why they share a symbol.

The book's word for it. Devore calls this a "conceptual population" (p. 111): when there is no real population, the pmf is treated as a model of one.

The last paragraph, in practice. If the experiment is "pick one member of a real population at random and measure it", then each value's probability is exactly its share of the population. The real population is already idealized, and is its ordinary mean. The small example below shows this.

The board reads "If we we studying"; "are" is supplied in brackets.

4The variance of a random variable

Let's define the variance of so that it is the variance of the idealized population for .

We will use , , , or to denote the variance of .

Definition
✎ Explanation (added)

Where the first line comes from. In an idealized population of members, the value occurs times. Lecture 2's population variance is : square each member's distance from the mean, add, divide by . Grouping equal values gives the top line, and the 's cancel just as they did for .

Why the divisor is and not . This is a population variance. The from Lecture 2 belongs to the sample variance , where a sample is being used to estimate . A pmf describes the whole population.

The last equals sign is Note 2 with : the variance is the expected squared distance from the mean.

6A dice game: is it fair?

Example

Example You are playing a simple dice game that costs $2 per play. You roll a fair six sided die and are awarded a payout based on the number roll.

If you roll a 1, 2, or 3, you get a payout of $0.
If you roll a 4 or a 5, you get a payout of $1.
If you roll a 6, you get a payout of $10.

Is this a fair game? Is the expected payout equal to the cost to play?

Let measure the payout we get.

Possible values can assign to outcomes: 0, 1, 10.

Distribution table:

00
1
10

This is a fair game.

✎ Explanation (added)

Where the probabilities come from. The six faces are equally likely. Three of them (1, 2, 3) pay $0, two (4, 5) pay $1, and one (6) pays $10, so the probabilities are , , ; they add to 1. Then .

What "fair" means here. The expected payout equals the $2 cost, so in the long run neither side comes out ahead. Equivalently, your net gain per play is , and by rule 5 of the next section .

Fair does not mean you usually break even. You lose money on 5 plays out of 6. The spread shows how uneven it is:

so and dollars.

✎ Explanation (added)

How to read ④–⑦. is the random variable you get by multiplying every value of by (a change of units, for example dollars to cents with ). adds to every value (a shift). The probabilities stay where they were.

  • Stretching by moves the mean by the same factor (④) and multiplies every distance from the mean by , so squared distances get multiplied by (⑥).
  • Shifting by moves the mean by (⑤) and moves every value along with it, so no distance from the mean changes (⑦).

The two combined rules on the right come from using a multiply rule and then a shift rule: , and .

One more consequence, not on the board. Taking the square root of the last rule gives . The absolute value matters when is negative: a standard deviation is never negative.

Example

Example You sell bags of apples and charge 50¢ per apple and 10¢ for the bag.

Let count the number of apples in a bag.
The mean number of apples per bag is 20.

What is the expected price you will charge for a bag of apples?

Let give the amount you charge for a bag of apples (in cents).

We need to find (with noted at the right)

✎ Explanation (added)

Setting it up. A bag with apples costs 50¢ for each apple plus 10¢ once, so . This is with and .

Why no pmf is needed. "The mean number of apples per bag is 20" is . The combined rule needs only that one number: cents, and . We are never told how the number of apples is distributed, and it does not matter.

If the spread were asked. Suppose we were also told apples (my number, not the board's). Then and cents = $1.00. The 10¢ for the bag shifts every price equally, so it has no effect on the spread.

What the book has that the board did not. Example 3.19 (p. 111) finds an expected value for a variable with infinitely many values, the number of births up to the first boy, and gets ; this is Lecture 7's "flip until the first head" with , so the expected number of flips is 2. Example 3.20 (p. 111) shows a pmf whose expected value is not finite (a "heavy tail"). Every board example had finitely many values, where neither issue arises.

Textbook examples worth reading

  • Example 3.16, p. 110. The expected number of courses for the 15,000-student population; a seven-value pmf pushed through the definition. It also points out that the mean is not the plain average of the possible values.
  • Example 3.22, p. 112. A cost that depends on a three-valued . It finds the pmf of the cost first and then shows the same answer comes from weighting by . This is why Note 2 works.
  • Example 3.23, pp. 112–113. A store's profit from selling computers turns out to be a linear function of ; the expected profit is found from the four-value pmf, and then again on p. 113 from alone. The same pattern as the apples.
  • Examples 3.24 and 3.25, pp. 114–115. One six-value pmf (DVDs checked out): the variance from the definition, then from the shortcut, with the same answer. Good practice for the table method.
  • Example 3.26, p. 116. The variance and standard deviation of the profit in Example 3.23 using .

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Table question. Given a pmf (or a short story you turn into one), find , and , usually with the four-column table and the shortcut. The coin example is the model.
  • Small population. A handful of members with listed values, as with the 5 couples: build the distribution table for a randomly chosen member, then find (and ) and connect it to the population mean. Aran's note says to expect this, with an artificially small population.
  • Fair game. A game with a cost and payouts: define , find its pmf, compute the expected payout and say whether the game is fair.
  • Linear rule. Given and maybe , find , or for a described , as with the apples.
  • Proof. Show one of rules 4 to 7, or derive the shortcut , starting from rules 1 and 2. Aran's note says to expect proofs like these or the ones in the tutorial.
  • Function of X. Compute something like from a table by replacing each , not each probability.
